To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the morphogenesis of the hind legs of honeybees is completed at brown-eyed pupa and is driven by a differential expression pattern of genes, including Hox proteins, that respond to different diets.
the hind leg phenotype determination in honeybees takes place between the 4th and 5th larval instars and that it is driven by a caste-specific gene expression profile, which includes Hox genes.

the development of honeybee worker and queen hind legs is driven by a combination of differentially expressed genes, including those encoding cuticular proteins, P450 and Ubx, in response to naturally different diets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the genetic basis of the honeybee caste differentiation and its implications in the evolution of eusociality.
the identification of genes involved in honeybee hind legs morphogenesis and the understanding of the molecular basis of the hind legs caste specific phenotype.
the molecular mechanisms that control the development of the worker hind leg, which has been previously described as a model for the evolution of worker caste.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hind legs morphological diphenism of A. mellifera is the result of the differential regulation of a set of genes that act at different developmental stages.

the morphogenetic differences observed between the hind leg of workers and queens of A. mellifera are driven by the expression of a set of caste specific genes, such as cuticular protein genes (CPR), cytochrome P450 and HOM-C genes, in response to naturally different diets during the larval stage.
the morphogenesis of honeybee hind leg phenotype is determined by a combination of genetic and nutritional factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Hox genes expression leads to differential leg development between honeybee castes.
the hind leg development is driven by a complex genetic cascade in which the Hox gene, Ubx, has a key role.
the differential expression of a set of genes, mainly those encoding Hox proteins, leads to the differential development of the hind leg between honeybee castes.
The main takeaway from our work is that

honeybees, as other social insects, are able to use a set of genes, including those coding for Hox transcription factors and P450 enzymes, to generate a caste specific morphology in response to different larval diets.
the hind legs of honeybees represent a model to study the genetic basis of morphological differences between castes.
the hind leg diphenism in A. mellifera is not the consequence of the loss of the corbicula in queens, but rather of the development of this specialized structure in workers.
